cues.text: Before calculating, let's picture it. An equation in three variables is a plane in space. Our three planes meet at a single point, and that point is the solution.
Now apply our first row operation: R two becomes R two minus two R one. Watch the green plane.
It tilts to a new position, but it still passes through the same point. Why? If a point satisfies both R one and R two, it automatically satisfies R two minus two R one.
And the step can be undone: just add two R one back. So no solutions are gained, and none are lost. The solution set is preserved.
Next, R three minus R one, and then R three minus two R two. Look at the final plane: it is perfectly flat. Seven z equals twenty-one, which is the plane z equals three.
Every step moved the planes, but never the meeting point. That is the whole idea behind Gaussian elimination.
